title: Welsh Cakes
subtitle: Griddle-cooked currant cakes from Wales
excerpt: Small, thick griddle cakes made with a buttery scone-like dough studded with currants and spiced with mixed spice, cooked directly on a dry griddle until golden on both sides. Served warm, dusted with caster sugar.

recipe.sourceNotes: Welsh cakes (picau ar y maen, or 'cakes on the stone') are cooked on a bakestone or griddle rather than in an oven. They have been a Welsh staple since at least the 19th century and are associated with St David's Day (1 March), though they are eaten year-round. The bakestone is a heavy flat iron plate, now usually replaced by a cast-iron griddle or heavy frying pan. The dough is a cross between a scone and a shortbread, rolled thicker than a biscuit and cut into rounds. They are at their best eaten warm from the griddle, though they keep well for several days.

content.text: The griddle must be at the right temperature: too hot and the outside will burn before the inside cooks through; too cool and the cakes will be pale and dry. A medium-low heat is correct. The dough should be thick enough to require flipping once only and should take about 3 to 4 minutes per side. The cakes are done when they feel firm to the touch and sound hollow when tapped on the base.
Rub the butter into the flour until it resembles fine breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar, currants, mixed spice, and salt.
Add the beaten egg and enough milk to bring the dough together into a soft but not sticky ball. Do not overwork it.
Roll out on a lightly floured surface to about 1 cm thick. Cut into rounds with a 6 cm cutter.

Cook in batches on a dry, ungreased griddle or heavy frying pan over medium-low heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and firm to the touch. Dust with caster sugar while still warm. Serve immediately or cool on a rack.
